title: United States v. Algernon Blair, Inc.
summary: A subcontractor that justifiably stopped after the prime contractor’s material breach could recover the reasonable value of its supplied labor and equipment, even though completing the subcontract would have produced a loss.
notes: The notes identify disagreement over using the contract price as a ceiling. They contrast Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 373 with Restatement (Third) of Restitution and Unjust Enrichment § 38(2)(b), and separately discuss the limitation after full performance. The case’s rule should not erase those qualifications.

sections.Parties: Coastal Steel Erectors was the subcontractor seeking payment in the name of the United States under the Miller Act. Algernon Blair was the prime contractor, and United States Fidelity and Guaranty Company was its surety.
sections.Material Facts:
Blair contracted to build a naval hospital and subcontracted steel erection and associated equipment to Coastal. Coastal supplied labor and its own cranes. Blair refused to pay crane rental, although the trial court found that the subcontract required payment. After approximately twenty-eight percent of the work, Coastal stopped because of that refusal. Blair finished with another subcontractor.

The trial court calculated approximately $37,000 otherwise due under the subcontract after prior payments, but found that Coastal would have lost more than that amount had it completed the job. Coastal sought the value of the labor and equipment already furnished rather than the profit it would have earned on full contractual performance.
sections.Procedural History: The district court found a material breach justifying Coastal’s termination but denied recovery after deducting the loss Coastal would have suffered on completion. The Fourth Circuit reversed in 1973 and remanded to determine the reasonable value of the benefits supplied, less amounts already paid.
sections.Issue: Must a subcontractor’s restitution recovery after justified termination be reduced by the loss it would have suffered had the losing contract been completed?
sections.Holding: No. Coastal could recover in quantum meruit—the reasonable value of the services and equipment furnished—without the deduction for its expected contractual loss. The contract price could inform value but did not cap recovery under this decision.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated restitution as an alternative basis of recovery after Blair’s material breach. Blair had received labor and the use of equipment without fully paying for those benefits. Coastal could elect to recover their reasonable value instead of claiming the net expectation produced by the contract’s remaining terms.

The reasonable value was the amount for which comparable performance could have been purchased from a supplier in Coastal’s position at the time and place of performance. This measure concerns the benefit provided, not simply Coastal’s expenditures. Because the trial court had not made the necessary valuation findings, reversal did not establish a final dollar award. Prior payments had to be credited to prevent a double recovery.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This case separates restitution from both expectation and reliance. It is especially useful when a plaintiff has partly performed a contract that would have lost money.

topics.restitution: Awards the reasonable value of a benefit conferred after the recipient materially breaches.
topics.remedies: Allows restitution even when the expectation measure is reduced to nothing by an expected loss.
topics.conditions: Material breach justified stopping work before complete performance.

mnemonic.rationale: A crane the contractor would not pay for
